stories.headline: Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s new biology skills wow scientists
stories.claim: OpenAI says its GPT-6.2 model designed proteins that bound five targets in lab tests, rivalling specialised biology AI.
stories.summary: OpenAI says its latest GPT-6 family model, GPT-6.2, helped design proteins that bound to five targets in laboratory tests, suggesting general-purpose AI models can carry out protein design without specialised biology tools. Coverage of the claim describes a hit rate of about 10.9% for minibinders in lab tests. The announcement has impressed scientists and puts pressure on specialist tools such as Google DeepMind's AlphaFold, which transformed protein structure prediction. Anthropic's Claude has also been cited in the same debate about general models' biology skills. The results are company-reported and await independent peer review, but they signal that frontier chatbots are moving into drug and protein research.

Reported minibinder hit rate in the lab is about 10.9%.

stories.headline: Huang's return to Nvidia brings open-weight AI debate to forefront in Washington
stories.claim: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO after his resignation; Trump and Vance reportedly intervened, spotlighting the open-weight AI debate.
stories.summary: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on 23 November, days after he resigned amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected of spying for China. Reuters reports that President Trump and Vice-President J.D. Vance personally intervened, seeing Huang as a protector of US-made open-weight AI models. Huang had lobbied Washington to back American open-weight developers, which would widen demand for Nvidia's chips. The White House called support for open-weight models its clear and long-standing policy, but declined to link that to Huang's reinstatement. Critics warn that political pressure on Huang could herald a crackdown on open-weight models.

stories.headline: Inside Fashion’s $276 Billion Succession Shakeup
stories.claim: Report says succession problems at family-owned fashion firms put $276bn of revenue at stake and could reshape the industry.
stories.summary: A new FashionSights report argues that generational handovers at family-owned fashion companies could reshape the industry's competitive map over the next decade. Its author, Achim Berg, a former McKinsey partner who founded the advisory boutique FashionSights in 2025, says 46 of the world's 100 largest fashion and apparel companies are family-controlled. Of those, 30 face a succession challenge, generating a combined $276bn in 2025 revenue, with 63% of them based in Europe. The findings come from an excerpt of a book he co-wrote, due in March from Bocconi University Press. Berg expects succession to drive consolidation, with Italian luxury groups, beauty and eyewear groups such as L'Oréal and EssilorLuxottica, and licensing firms like ABG as likely buyers. He says successions typically need 10 to 15 years of planning, and cites Zegna as a positive example.

Those 30 companies generated a combined $276bn in revenue in 2025.
63% of the at-risk companies are in Europe, 30% in North America and 7% in Asia-Pacific.

L'Oréal, EssilorLuxottica and licensing firms such as ABG, WHP Global and Marquee Brands are named as possible buyers.

stories.headline: Bangladesh Garment Workers Clash With Police Amid Wage Negotiations
stories.claim: Bangladeshi police fired tear gas at thousands of garment workers protesting over stalled minimum-wage talks.
stories.summary: Bangladeshi police fired tear gas and stun grenades at thousands of garment workers who blocked the main Dhaka to Mymensingh highway on Tuesday after a wage board meeting was postponed. Protesters hurled bricks and torched vehicles, and about 500 of the country's 4,500 garment factories are reportedly shut. Workers want a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($240), up 140% from 12,500 taka, to cope with rising living costs. The sector, the world's second-biggest garment exporter after China, is worth $38bn a year and employs more than four million people. The government's wage board will announce a new minimum wage in December, to take effect in January. Border Guard Bangladesh has increased patrols across industrial zones.

stories.headline: EU launches antitrust probe into Coca-Cola bottler
stories.claim: The European Commission opened an antitrust investigation into Coca-Cola Europacific Partners over cross-border pricing practices.
stories.summary: The European Commission has opened an antitrust investigation into Coca-Cola Europacific Partners, one of Coca-Cola's largest European bottlers, over claims it stopped retailers buying drinks cheaply in other EU countries. Regulators suspect the bottler offered discounts on condition that retailers did not resell the drinks elsewhere in the EU. The probe will also examine whether bottle and can sizes were varied between countries to hinder cross-border trade, and whether the company paid retailers to limit soft drink imports into Spain. The Commission raided the company's offices in March 2025. If the case is proven, CCEP could face a fine of up to 10% of its global annual turnover, and there is no deadline for the inquiry. The company said it takes competition law very seriously and will cooperate fully.

stories.headline: China launches Shenzhou-24 carrying first foreign astronaut, a Pakistani, to Tiangong
stories.claim: China launched Shenzhou-24 on 25 November carrying Pakistani payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreign national to visit Tiangong.
stories.summary: China launched the Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on 25 November at 8.18am Beijing time, carrying Pakistani pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali to the Tiangong space station. Ali, 40, is the first foreign national to visit the station and the first Pakistani in orbit. He flies with Chinese commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi aboard the spacecraft, which rode a Long March-2F rocket. Ali will serve as a payload specialist and stay for five to 10 days, running more than 90 experiments, including a photosynthetic cyanobacteria study, before returning on Shenzhou-23. He trained for seven months in Beijing, including Chinese-language study and calligraphy. The flight stems from a China-Pakistan space agreement signed in February 2025 and underlines Beijing's push to position Tiangong as an international cooperation hub as the ISS nears retirement around 2030. China aims for a crewed lunar landing by 2030, while NASA targets 2028 for its own Moon landing.

stories.summary: Survivors of the Wang Fuk Court estate in Tai Po are marking the first anniversary of the fire that killed 168 people, the deadliest blaze in Hong Kong since 1948, and many say they still feel no justice has been done. Many former residents plan to return to the estate on Thursday to mourn. The blaze tore through seven of the estate's eight 31-storey blocks, which had been wrapped in scaffolding and netting for renovation work. Last month, leader John Lee published an independent report that partly blamed four government departments and accepted the resignation of Housing Secretary Winnie Ho, the first official to step down over the fire. Lee also promised reforms, including laws to criminalise bid rigging in the renovation industry. The government has ruled out rebuilding on the original site and offered a buyback scheme, which most owners have accepted, but survivors such as Yip Ka Kui, whose wife died, say it does little to ease their sense of injustice. Authorities have ruled out commemorative events, though the Chief Secretary says lawful gatherings are permitted and destructive acts will be prosecuted.

stories.headline: Australia and Solomon Islands sign security treaty, a blow to China's Pacific influence
stories.claim: Australia and the Solomon Islands signed a sweeping security treaty in Canberra, naming Australia primary security partner and ruling out foreign bases.
stories.summary: Australia and the Solomon Islands signed a sweeping security treaty in Canberra on 25 November 2026, making Australia the island nation's "primary security partner" and ruling out any foreign military or security base on Solomon soil. Prime Minister Matthew Wale and 15 ministers attended the signing, which is widely seen as a counterweight to China's growing footprint in the Pacific. Australia will commit AU$740 million (about US$490 million) over ten years, including AU$670 million in grants and AU$70 million in concessional loans, for education, health, policing and climate resilience. The treaty bars militarisation or foreign interference in sensitive infrastructure such as airports, ports, energy and telecoms, but the clause is not retroactive, so existing Chinese-built assets are not covered. Wale is trying to unwind close ties with Beijing built under his predecessor Manasseh Sogavare, and said talks with China are ongoing; the 2022 China security pact is still being discussed and he cannot comment on it because of a non-disclosure clause. The opposition criticised the fast-tracking, and parliament returns in January to approve reforms.

stories.headline: Tiny licence-free cars boom across Europe as teenagers and rural drivers buy in
stories.claim: Licence-free mini-cars are booming across Europe, with sales doubling in five years and teenagers and rural drivers buying in.
stories.summary: Europe's licence-free mini-cars are enjoying a sharp rise in popularity, with European sales doubling from about 30,000 to 60,000 over the past five years. In France, registrations roughly doubled from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year. Teenagers now account for a quarter of mini-car sales, and young people make up around 40% of French maker Ligier's customers. The growth has been driven in part by stricter EU rules that made mopeds too costly for manufacturers to certify, pushing buyers towards these vehicles, which top out at 45km/h and are banned from motorways. Stellantis's Citroën Ami, launched in 2020, has given the segment wider visibility, and according to AAA Data more than 67% of new licence-free cars sold in 2026 are electric. Aixam has put €30m into expanding French production capacity, though French sales have flattened since electric subsidies were withdrawn.

stories.headline: Huawei convicted of fraud and trade-secret theft in US trial over Iran business
stories.claim: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud and trade-secret conspiracy, and acquitted it of racketeering.
stories.summary: A Brooklyn federal jury has convicted Chinese telecoms giant Huawei on 10 of 12 criminal counts, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets from American companies. The verdict came on Tuesday, 24 November, after a trial of more than two months with over 60 prosecution witnesses. Jurors acquitted the company of its most serious charge, racketeering conspiracy, and of conspiring to obstruct justice, a result Huawei's lawyer Brian Heberlig called a vindication. Prosecutors said Huawei lied to banks about business in Iran and North Korea and built its business on theft, citing incidents involving T-Mobile, Cisco and Quintel. The case dates to 2018, when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, and to charges announced in 2019. Judge Ann Donnelly will sentence the company on 14 September 2027, with potential penalties running into billions of dollars. Huawei says it fully expects to appeal, and experts say the case has not hurt its business, which has grown in China's AI push.

stories.headline: Tech giants to face billions of dollars in fines under Australian internet safety bill

stories.summary: Australia has set out a sharply tougher version of its Digital Duty of Care bill, threatening internet companies including Google and Meta with fines of up to 5% of global revenue. The change follows a deal with the Greens in the Senate and lifts the potential penalty well above the previously proposed A$109 million ($72.2 million). The law would replace a patchwork of industry codes with one statute requiring platforms to proactively detect and remove harmful content, including child sexual abuse material and terrorism content. It would also let individuals sue platforms for enabling wrongdoing. Communications Minister Anika Wells said the bill would be debated in parliament this week. Tech firms broadly back the goals but oppose the discretion the bill gives officials over what counts as harmful content, and the deal means the bill is on track to become law.

stories.headline: Mexico captures FBI most-wanted cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro'; can it dismantle his cartel?
stories.claim: Mexican forces captured cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro' in a raid in Sinaloa; analysts question whether the cartel can be dismantled.
stories.summary: Mexico's military captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as 'El Chapo Isidro' and one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, in a special forces raid in Guasave, Sinaloa, on Friday night. The operation, which Mexico's defence ministry said had US intelligence support, triggered gunfights, burning vehicles and roadblocks across Sinaloa, easing by Saturday. Two other alleged gang leaders, including his second-in-command, were arrested with him and flown to Mexico City for prosecutors. Security forces said seven attackers were killed, eight suspects were arrested and four Mexican soldiers died. Meza Flores was indicted in the US in 2012, carries a US$5m reward, and is accused of trafficking heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and fentanyl. The capture is a significant blow to the Beltrán Leyva group, though a follow-up analysis notes that cartels remain deeply embedded in Mexican politics and the economy.

stories.headline: US Army to detonate about five tonnes of toxic lead azide in Iowa after court clears plan
stories.claim: US Army to detonate about five tonnes of lead azide at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday after appeals court clears the plan.
stories.summary: The US Army is set to detonate about five tonnes of degraded lead azide, a volatile compound, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday morning. The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals declined on Monday to block the operation, finding an emergency and adequate safeguards in place. The detonation has already been postponed three times, and President Trump had earlier paused it until courts and incoming Democratic governor Rob Sand agreed. Sand has not said whether he supports the move, while the current governor, Kim Reynolds, backs it. Environmental groups, including the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, warned of a plume of toxic lead particles and accused the government of bypassing the courts, arguing the EPA had not weighed the risks. The EPA issued an emergency permit covering 68 drums, citing an imminent threat to health and the environment. Officials say the material has degraded and that cold weather raises the risk of an uncontrolled explosion, which is why they consider it too unstable to store.

stories.headline: US blacklists Singapore-based Megaspeed and six firms over alleged Nvidia chip diversion
stories.claim: The US Commerce Department added Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other Southeast Asian firms to its Entity List, requiring licences for advanced US chips.
stories.summary: The US Commerce Department added Singapore-based Megaspeed International and six other Southeast Asian firms to its Entity List on Monday 23 November, the same day Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia chief executive. Listed firms now need a US licence to receive advanced American technology, including Nvidia's top AI GPUs, and applications are likely to be denied. The department said it suspected Megaspeed of routing Nvidia chips to Chinese companies in breach of export controls after almost two years of investigation. Three of the listed companies are in Malaysia, one in Thailand and two in Singapore. Singapore's prime minister Lawrence Wong said his government is working with Washington on an enforcement mechanism, while saying Singapore lacks full information on chip end users. Malaysia's trade ministry will advise data centre operators not to host or serve the blacklisted firms, though this is advice rather than a ban. China has warned against a technological blockade.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump push; shares surge
stories.claim: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and president on 23 November, after US government input and Trump's push; shares surged about 30%.
stories.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive and president with immediate effect on Monday 23 November, less than two weeks after he resigned, saying US government input indicated his return poses no national security risk. Nvidia shares jumped roughly 30 per cent at the open, adding close to $1tn in market value and lifting the Nasdaq and Dow sharply. The reversal followed a campaign in which President Trump said he 'made the deal' by pressing the board, including by phone during a board meeting, and JD Vance reportedly reassured directors. Huang had stepped down on 12 November after admitting an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive whom US intelligence has reportedly linked to a Chinese espionage network, and he was also reported to have had an affair with an Nvidia executive. Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will remain chief financial officer. Bipartisan lawmakers, including Senator Elizabeth Warren, have demanded answers, while the SEC and Department of Justice investigations and an independent board probe into security and intellectual property leakage continue. The episode underscores how closely investors and policymakers watch Nvidia, the world's most valuable chipmaker.
key_points: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, president and director with immediate effect on 23 November.
The board said US government input indicated his return poses no national security risk and that it was satisfied with his candour and ability to lead.
Nvidia shares closed about 31 per cent higher, adding nearly $1tn in market value, while the Nasdaq rose about 6.4 per cent.
Trump said he 'made the deal' and pressed the board, and reports say VP JD Vance held a private call with Huang and reassured directors.
Huang resigned on 12 November after admitting an affair with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence has reportedly linked to China, and a second affair reportedly involving an Nvidia executive.
Colette Kress remains CFO, while the SEC, Department of Justice and an independent board probe continue, and Senator Warren demanded answers from Huang and Nvidia.
stories.market_take: Investors see Huang's return as a sign of continuity for Nvidia, which is a bellwether for the AI chip trade.

stories.headline: Amazon buys AI accelerator technology and staff from Israeli startup Decart
stories.claim: Amazon has agreed to acquire Decart's AI optimisation technology and its founders and engineers in a deal Bloomberg values at about $7.5bn; neither company has confirmed a price.
stories.summary: Amazon has agreed to acquire the proprietary AI optimisation technology of Israeli startup Decart, along with its three founders and engineering team, in a deal Bloomberg reports is valued at around $7.5 billion. The move follows earlier reports, from November, that Amazon was closing in on a deal of about $7.5bn including cash, stock and performance earnouts, with the Wall Street Journal first reporting talks around $7bn in October. Amazon describes the deal as an asset purchase rather than a whole-company takeover, so Decart's other models are not included and the startup's future is unclear. Neither company has disclosed a price. The Decart Optimization Stack sits between AI models and chips, tuning kernels, compilers and runtimes so accelerators stay fully utilised, and it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs and AWS Trainium chips. Amazon SVP Peter DeSantis framed the deal as a way to push Trainium and its AI efforts further. If the Bloomberg figure holds, it would rank among Amazon's largest acquisitions, behind its $8.5 billion purchase of MGM. The deal underlines Amazon's push to cut inference costs and make its own chips more competitive. Decart raised $300m in May 2026 at roughly a $4bn valuation.
key_points: Amazon has agreed to buy Decart's Optimization Stack technology and bring on its three founders and engineering team.
Bloomberg reports the deal is valued at around $7.5 billion; neither company has confirmed a price.
The deal is an asset purchase, so Decart's other technology is not included and its future is unclear.
The software supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs and AWS Trainium chips, keeping accelerators fully utilised.
Earlier reports had put talks at about $7bn, and Anthropic's roughly $6bn talks collapsed in September.
Decart raised $300m in May 2026 at roughly a $4bn valuation.
stories.market_take: A reported $7.5bn outlay is modest for Amazon's scale, but it signals a push to improve Trainium economics against Nvidia.

stories.headline: Japan opposition parties to submit motion to censure scandal-hit minister
stories.claim: Japan's opposition parties agreed to file a censure motion against education minister Yoshihiro Seki and to boycott a consumption tax cut bill.
stories.summary: Japan's opposition parties have agreed to submit a censure motion against education minister Yoshihiro Seki over a fundraising scandal, and to boycott deliberations on a key consumption tax cut bill. Senior officials from six opposition parties in the Senate reached the decision on Tuesday, with the motion possibly tabled this week. The scandal centres on revelations that senior bureaucrats gave presentations at Seki's fundraising parties, blurring official duties and political fundraising. Because the opposition holds a majority in the upper house, the censure motion could pass, though it would not be legally binding. The move threatens Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's plan to cut the consumption tax on food and drink for two years from April, as the current session ends on 12 December. Seki says he intends to stay on.

The opposition has agreed to boycott deliberations on the consumption tax cut bill for now.

stories.headline: Asian stocks rally as Huang's return to Nvidia revives the AI trade
stories.claim: Asian shares surged on 24 November after Huang's return revived the AI trade, with Nvidia up 31.5% the day before.
stories.summary: Asian stocks leapt on Monday's session's aftermath as Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO sparked a relief rally in the battered AI trade. Taiwan's shares jumped 9.1% from an eight-month low, with TSMC and Foxconn both near their daily limit of about 10%. MSCI's broadest Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index rose 4%, Japan's Nikkei rose as much as 5%, and South Korea's KOSPI surged 6.5%. Nvidia shares surged 31.5% on 23 November, their biggest daily gain in 23 years, restoring nearly US$1 trillion in value. Chinese shares lagged on fears of tighter US chip export curbs, and futures pointed to some easing of the euphoria, while the rally has raised bets on a Fed rate hike in December.
key_points: Taiwan's market rose 9.1% from an eight-month low, with TSMC and Foxconn near their daily limits.
MSCI's Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index rose 4%, its biggest one-day gain since 31 July.
Nvidia shares rose 31.5% on 23 November, the biggest daily percentage gain in 23 years.
Chinese shares lagged, with the CSI 300 up 0.6% and Hong Kong down 0.4%, on concerns about tighter US chip export curbs.
Fed funds futures now price a December hike as near certain, compared with 89% odds on 27 November, according to CME FedWatch.
stories.market_take: The rebound lifts AI chip names across Asia, but traders now see a December Fed hike as near certain, which is a headwind for equities.

stories.headline: Oil holds near three-month low as rising supply offsets Hormuz threat
stories.claim: Oil held near a three-month low on Tuesday as rising supply and expected surplus outweighed Hormuz shipping risks.
stories.summary: Oil prices hovered near a three-month low on Tuesday, with Brent at $88.97 a barrel, after posting their lowest close since 31 August on Monday. WTI was at $79.94, its lowest since late August. Rising supply, including Libya's restored Sharara pipeline flows, is weighing on prices, and Deutsche Bank estimates global observed inventories rose by 52 million barrels in October, implying a daily surplus of 1.7 million barrels. Risks persist, however: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and US authorities are investigating possible Iranian involvement in cyberattacks on as many as 50 energy tankers. Analysts at ANZ say the market remains fragile with thin inventory buffers.

Both benchmarks were near their lowest levels since late August.
Deutsche Bank sees global inventories rising and a surplus of about 1.7 million barrels a day in October.
Libya's Sharara pipeline has reopened, adding supply.
Naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and cyberattacks on tankers are keeping risk premium in the market.
stories.market_take: Oil is soft on supply and surplus expectations, but Hormuz risk could quickly reverse the decline.

stories.headline: Prosecutors say ex-OpenAI engineer secretly recorded meetings and likely captured trade secrets
stories.claim: US prosecutors say former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan secretly recorded meetings and likely captured trade secrets; he has pleaded not guilty.
stories.summary: US prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, hid a recording device behind a television in an executive conference room and likely intercepted trade secrets. In a 23 November court filing, they said they found hundreds of audio files on his personal computer, including dozens of recordings of OpenAI meetings from September 2026. Some recordings were uploaded to Dropbox, and he kept a photo of a confidential 'strategic partnership' term sheet between OpenAI and another company. Alfozan, a US green card holder, was fired on the day of his October arrest and has pleaded not guilty to the eavesdropping charge. Prosecutors are urging the court to keep him in custody, arguing he could flee to Saudi Arabia, while Judge Vince Chhabria has voiced concern about whether he should remain detained. The case highlights the security of confidential information at a leading AI developer.

stories.headline: AI stock rout hits Asian markets; Hong Kong hits 19-month low
stories.claim: Hong Kong stocks hit a 19-month low on Monday as a rout in US AI shares spread across Asian markets.
stories.summary: Hong Kong's stock market slid to its lowest level in 19 months on Monday as a rout in US artificial intelligence shares spilled into Asia. The Hang Seng Tech Index fell as much as 3 per cent to below 3,400 points and is down more than a third for the year, while the broader Hang Seng Index dropped as much as 1.8 per cent intraday. Earlier, the Nasdaq lost 10% in the previous week, its worst weekly drop since March 2020, and Taiwan's benchmark posted its sharpest weekly fall since 1990. South Korean shares fell about 4% before partly recovering. Investors are questioning whether heavy borrowing to fund AI data-centre spending can pay off quickly enough to support debt and high valuations. In response, Taiwan tightened short-selling rules, Chinese exchanges eased margin-financing requirements, and South Korea's finance minister was due to discuss a possible market stabilisation fund. US futures rebounded early Monday, with Nasdaq 100 futures up nearly 3%, though gains were uneven.

stories.claim: Trump hosts his third gala for top $TRUMP meme coin holders on Sunday night as their holdings have collapsed.
stories.summary: President Donald Trump is hosting a gala dinner at Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, on Sunday night for the top holders of his $TRUMP meme coin, his third such event. The top 185 holders are invited to dinner, the top 29 to a VIP reception, and the top four receive gold watches. Guests include Floyd Mayweather, Kevin O'Leary, Tristan Thompson and Lior Suchard. Interest has collapsed, with the combined holdings of contestants falling from $148m in May 2025 to $8.6m for this month's gala. Democrats, including Senator Adam Schiff, say the dinners let the president profit from his office and have promised investigations and legislation to ban such events. The White House calls it a private event and says no official action is promised in return. Reuters analysis found outside investors in five Trump crypto-linked projects lost more than $5bn, and disclosures show more than $1bn of crypto income since Trump returned to office.

stories.headline: Democrats win largest US House majority since 1992, with about 259 seats
stories.claim: Democrats win their largest US House majority since 1992, with at least 258 seats after Chuck Hubbard unseated Virginia Foxx.
stories.summary: Democrats have secured their largest majority in the US House since 1992, with CNN projecting 259 seats in the 435-member chamber. The party reached at least 258 seats on Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard beat Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx by 330 votes in North Carolina's 5th district. Foxx, who had held the seat since 2005, requested a recount under state law and then conceded. Republicans hold at least 173 seats, with four races still uncalled, including contests in Minnesota and Tennessee, and two Louisiana seats heading to a 12 December runoff. The party's net gain of around 40 to 44 seats would be the third-largest in half a century, behind 2010 and 1994. Democrats also control the Senate with a 56-seat majority, creating divided government under President Donald Trump. Voters cited high prices, the war with Iran and corruption concerns. Democrats plan a 100-day agenda from January on living costs, healthcare and immigration, including investigating the administration and blocking cabinet nominees, though Trump retains veto power.

stories.headline: COP31 talks in Antalya collapse over fossil fuel language; draft omits coal, oil and gas
stories.claim: COP31 talks in Antalya collapsed on Monday after more than two weeks of deadlock over fossil fuel and climate finance language.
stories.summary: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed on Monday after more than two weeks of contentious talks, making it the longest-ever UN climate negotiations, with countries unable to agree on fossil fuels or on money. Earlier, on the Sunday of overtime talks, the latest draft from the Turkish and Australian presidency again avoided naming coal, oil or gas, instead referring to the 2023 Dubai consensus on moving away from fossil fuels. About 130 countries, backed by the EU, wanted explicit transition language, while Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich states opposed it, and the EU raised the prospect of 'no deal'. Tuvalu's climate minister called the fossil fuel reference a red line. Other disputes included carbon capture and storage and a target for electricity to reach 35% of final energy by 2035. Developing nations objected to the removal of a US$120 billion climate adaptation target, and some delegates left, raising quorum concerns. Campaigners called it the 'worst COP ever', pointing to Berkeley Earth's finding that October 2026 was the warmest October on record. The breakdown undermines the idea of broad consensus on phasing out fossil fuels, a key goal of global climate diplomacy.
key_points: The longest-ever UN climate negotiations, COP31 in Antalya, collapsed on Monday without agreement on fossil fuels or climate finance.
The talks had been scheduled to end on Friday and ran into days of overtime.
The draft text avoided naming coal, oil or gas, referring instead to the 2023 Dubai consensus.
About 130 countries, backed by the EU, sought explicit phase-out language, while Saudi Arabia and allied oil producers opposed it.
Developing nations objected to removing a US$120 billion climate adaptation target, and some delegates left, risking quorum.
Campaigners called the summit the 'worst COP ever', noting October 2026 was the warmest October on record per Berkeley Earth.

stories.headline: Asian regulators roll out emergency measures as AI-driven stock rout hits Kospi and chipmakers
stories.claim: Regulators in China, South Korea and Taiwan have rolled out emergency measures to contain an AI-driven stock rout that has hit Asian chip shares.
stories.summary: Authorities in China, South Korea and Taiwan have introduced emergency measures to stem market turmoil triggered by a global sell-off in artificial-intelligence stocks. South Korea's KOSPI had plunged about 5% on Monday 23 November as concerns over the AI trade and a broader technology selloff deepened, and Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said stabilisation funds would be activated depending on market conditions. Taiwan had already widened short-sale curbs and state share buying after its index fell 5.65% in its steepest weekly drop since 1997. The sell-off followed a broader AI-led tech rout in the United States, where chipmakers such as Micron, Broadcom, Nvidia and AMD fell roughly 12% to 14% on Friday. Chipmakers and hardware suppliers in the region are the most exposed to shifts in AI sentiment. Investors are watching whether the intervention steadies prices or whether the selling continues.

stories.headline: US ports face cyber attack onslaught as hackers target vital trade routes
stories.claim: FT reports US ports face a rising flood of cyber intrusion attempts, with some shipping firms already suffering breaches.
stories.summary: US ports are facing a sustained wave of cyber intrusion attempts, with the Port of Corpus Christi, America's major crude export hub, reportedly seeing hundreds and sometimes thousands of attempts a day. The Financial Times reported on 22 November that attackers are increasingly targeting the systems that keep cargo, fuel and ships moving, and that some shipping firms have already suffered breaches. The scale of successful attacks and the specific ports affected remain unclear, and blocked login attempts should not be confused with compromises. The Port of Los Angeles has also described large volumes of blocked malicious activity. Disruption could delay energy exports and wider trade, so the story highlights growing cyber risk to critical infrastructure. US authorities, including the Coast Guard and the Maritime Administration, have issued guidance urging tighter access controls and better vulnerability management.

stories.headline: BepiColombo spacecraft enter orbit around Mercury despite thruster glitch
stories.claim: BepiColombo entered orbit around Mercury, but a software glitch cut short a key thruster burn; ESA says the mission remains on track.
stories.summary: Europe's and Japan's joint BepiColombo mission has entered orbit around Mercury, becoming only the third spacecraft to visit the planet and the second to orbit it. The European Space Agency said on Monday that the mission remains on track and the spacecraft is in a stable orbit, despite a software glitch that cut short a key thruster burn. The 37-minute burn, begun about 635 km above the surface, was interrupted early, so the craft achieved roughly 77% of the planned velocity change, and it entered safe mode for a time. The spacecraft had travelled more than eight years and about 6bn miles to reach Mercury. Further thruster burns are scheduled in coming months to adjust the orbit. The two orbiters are still due to separate on 9 December, with one European and one Japanese craft. Routine science operations are expected to begin in April, and the orbiters should last about three years. The €1.6bn mission aims to explain how Mercury formed so close to the Sun, why it has a magnetic field, and what ice lies in its permanently shadowed craters.

The spacecraft entered safe mode for a time after the glitch.

stories.headline: Anthropic shares slip after record IPO as AI-led tech rout pushes US indexes into correction
stories.claim: US indexes entered correction as an AI-led tech rout hit chipmakers and Anthropic shares slid after its record IPO.
stories.summary: Anthropic's record IPO has been overshadowed by a sharp AI-led tech sell-off that pushed the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory. The S&P 500 closed down 3.59% at 6,918.45 on Friday, its seventh straight losing session and longest such run since February 2020, while the Nasdaq erased all of its 2026 gains. Chipmakers led the drop, with Micron, Broadcom, Nvidia and AMD down roughly 12% to 14%, and the VIX topped 30. Anthropic sold 980 million shares at $83 in Thursday's IPO, raising about $81 billion, and opened at $111.50 before closing at $97.17 on debut; it fell about 9% on Friday to roughly $85 by midday. Investors are questioning returns on debt-funded AI spending, and worries have grown over tighter AI regulation after a Democratic sweep in the midterms. Asian markets were hit hard, with Taiwan's index down 5.65% and the Nikkei and Kospi each down about 5%.
key_points: The S&P 500 closed down 3.59% at 6,918.45 on Friday, its seventh straight losing session.
The Dow entered correction territory and the Nasdaq erased all of its 2026 gains.
Micron, Broadcom, Nvidia and AMD fell roughly 12% to 14%, and the VIX topped 30.
Anthropic sold 980 million shares at $83, raising about $81 billion, and fell about 9% on its second day of trading.
Taiwan's index fell 5.65% in its steepest weekly drop since 1997, while the Nikkei and Kospi each fell about 5%.
Concerns include debt-funded AI spending, Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO and possible tighter AI regulation.

stories.headline: Alice Huang chip-smuggling probe widens, drawing scrutiny of Nvidia and Lutnick
stories.claim: Scrutiny of Alice Huang's alleged chip network and Chinese intelligence ties has widened, with US senators and reports pressing Commerce and Treasury officials.
stories.summary: Scrutiny of Alice Huang, the Singapore-based former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia affair, has widened as new reporting links her to Chinese intelligence and to alleged chip smuggling. The Financial Times and New York Times have tied her to a network that moved Nvidia chips into China, with the NYT citing a Strider Technologies analysis linking about $3.6bn of Chinese state money to her family's companies. Recent reports say US intelligence tracked her contacts with China's Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 until this autumn, and her business partner Kang Wei is also under federal examination. Senator John Kennedy has demanded that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent testify under oath, accusing the commerce department of incompetence or complicity. Nvidia says it has stopped H200 shipments to China, while Beijing calls the spy allegations a smear and Huang denies Chinese intelligence links. Her claimed career history has not been independently confirmed. The case is intensifying pressure on export enforcement and Nvidia's internal compliance culture.

stories.headline: UK Workers Stay Put as Safety Trumps Pay in Perilous Jobs Market
stories.claim: UK workers are staying in their jobs, prioritising security over pay, as job switching falls to pre-pandemic levels.
stories.summary: British workers are clinging to their jobs and accepting flat or falling pay in exchange for security, a shift that shows how precarious the labour market feels. Official figures show only 2 million people changed roles in the first nine months of 2026, below pre-pandemic levels and almost 1 million fewer than in the same period of 2022. A YouGov poll for Employment Hero found that over 60 percent of workers now put job security ahead of earning more, up from 58 percent last year. Around half said their pay had fallen behind the cost of living. The Bank of England, which describes a low-fire, low-hire market, is watching whether this restrains wage growth as inflation is set to exceed 4 percent early next year. The Bloomberg piece itself was only partly visible, so detail is drawn from the other report.
key_points: Only 2 million people changed jobs in the first nine months of 2026, below pre-pandemic levels.
Over 60 percent of British workers prioritise job security over earning more, up from 58 percent last year.
A typical worker aged 35 or over estimates they missed out on £13,100 a year by not switching employers, according to YouGov polling for Employment Hero.
Around half of workers said their pay has fallen behind the cost of living.
Vacancies are at their lowest in over five years, and real wages are falling.
The Bank of England is watching for wage-price effects as inflation is expected to exceed 4 percent in early 2027.
stories.market_take: Weak labour mobility can ease wage pressure, which matters for UK rate expectations.

stories.headline: European firms warn EU leaders against budget cuts on competitiveness
stories.claim: Green energy and industrial groups urge EU leaders not to cut the European Competitiveness Fund in the 2028-2034 budget.
stories.summary: More than 75 European companies and industry bodies, including EDF and PowerCo, have written to EU leaders urging them not to cut the European Competitiveness Fund. The letter comes ahead of a Brussels summit on Thursday on the 2028-2034 budget, where summit chair Antonio Costa has proposed cutting the budget by €40 billion compared with October's Irish presidency proposal. Most of the cut falls on the competitiveness fund, along with defence and external spending. The groups say the fund is already trimmed by 10 percent to €356 billion in 2025 prices, far more than the 3 percent cut to farming and poorer regions. They want leaders to back the European Parliament's proposal to add €26.6 billion, with much of it for industrial decarbonisation. The dispute reflects a wider fight over how the bloc funds innovation and reduces its energy import dependence.

stories.headline: The Russia-Ukraine war is not a world war – yet
stories.claim: Ukrainian sea drones sank a Russian corvette and hit a cargo ship off Libya, as the Russia-Ukraine war spreads across seas.

Commentators argue the war is becoming global: two cargo ships were sunk off Bulgaria last week, and a drone strike hit the sanctioned Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland. The Black Sea, where Russia has tried to blockade Ukraine's trade, is now described as more dangerous than the Strait of Hormuz. Sabotage, drone incursions and cruise missiles hitting Poland have also been cited as signs of spillover. stories.headline: Rajan Warns AI Boom Faces a Reckoning on Returns
stories.claim: Raghuram Rajan warns that AI infrastructure spending may not earn adequate returns, risking oversupply and valuation pressure.
stories.summary: Former Reserve Bank of India governor Raghuram Rajan has warned that the AI boom could face a reckoning over returns, arguing that the huge sums spent on computing capacity may never earn back their cost. He says supply could outrun demand because businesses are slow to adopt existing AI tools, and he points to OpenAI's output of 722 research manuscripts on 377 unsolved maths problems as an example of research that does not yet produce revenue. Rajan says AI model advantages last only one to two months and that debt-financed firms are most exposed. He made the case in a Bloomberg interview and in a 18 November essay. It is an opinion from a respected economist rather than new data, but it adds to investor debate about AI spending, and US political calls to pause data-centre approvals add to the friction.

stories.headline: New ‘Planet X’ Theory Suggests Something Big Is Hiding Beyond Neptune
stories.claim: A new study proposes a possible 'Planet X2' of 1.5 to 2 Earth masses beyond Neptune to explain distant icy object orbits.
stories.summary: A new study in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society proposes that an undiscovered planet, dubbed Planet X2, could be orbiting far beyond Neptune, with between 1.5 and two times Earth's mass. The research, led by Patryk Sofia Lykawka, used computer simulations over about 4.5 billion years of solar system history. The hypothetical world would sit at 350 to 500 astronomical units on a highly elongated orbit, never coming closer than 200 AU to the Sun, compared with Neptune's roughly 30 AU. The model aims to explain odd orbits of distant bodies such as Sedna. It is separate from the better-known Planet Nine hypothesis, which posits a body of about 6.2 Earth masses.
key_points: The study was published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society and led by Patryk Sofia Lykawka.
Planet X2 is proposed to have between 1.5 and two times Earth's mass.
Simulations tested orbits with a semi-major axis of 350 to 500 AU, staying at least 200 AU from the Sun.
The model reproduced several observed patterns among distant objects, though differences with observations remain.
The idea is distinct from Planet Nine, which is modelled at about 6.2 Earth masses and 380 AU.
No observational detection of the planet has been reported.

stories.headline: Russian strikes kill at least nine in Dymer, Ukraine; boy rescued alive from rubble
stories.claim: Russian strikes killed at least ten people in Dymer, Ukraine, and a seven-year-old boy was pulled alive from rubble after about 14 hours.
stories.summary: Rescuers in Ukraine pulled a seven-year-old boy alive from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, after about 14 hours of work following a Russian strike. Ukrainian officials say the overnight attacks killed ten people in Dymer, and a 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive, while more than 130 emergency workers are at the scene. Zelensky described the five-storey block as largely destroyed. Across the Kyiv region and beyond, strikes killed one in Bila Tserkva and three in a Vyshneve grocery store, where 13 were wounded, and Ukraine's interior minister said more than 70 strikes were launched across 10 regions by Sunday evening. Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region. Separately, a Russian navy corvette, the Merkury, was severely damaged and sank in the Libyan port of Benghazi in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, more than 1,000 miles from Ukraine, though no one has claimed responsibility. stories.headline: Germany warns Russia may launch nuclear-armed satellite; NATO vows defence
stories.claim: German outlets report Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite within 60 days; NATO vows defence, but the claims are unconfirmed.

Rutte did not confirm the reports, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, speaking alongside him, neither confirmed nor denied them, saying they showed the escalation Russia was prepared to pursue. The reports cite anonymous German and Western intelligence that the satellite was assembled years ago and is stationed near Moscow, with warnings in early November that a launch could come within that window. The Kremlin called the claims speculative and said it had not seen the report, while the Russian embassy in Berlin dismissed them as unfounded propaganda. Berlin has not confirmed the reports and no official confirmation has been published. A launch would breach the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit, and the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty. The claims echo a 2024 US accusation that Russia was developing a nuclear anti-satellite weapon.

stories.headline: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo, open-source tool to defend against AI-driven attacks
stories.claim: Cisco and OpenAI have released Shirudo, an open-source eBPF tool that lets AI agents build temporary kernel-level shields for unpatched Linux systems.
stories.summary: Cisco and OpenAI have released Shirudo, an open-source tool that uses eBPF to apply temporary protections to Linux systems that cannot be patched quickly. The project was launched on 23 November 2026 as the number of software flaws surges, with more than 100,000 reported this year, many found by AI bug-hunting tools. Shirudo lets AI agents scan infrastructure and use OpenAI's Codex to write eBPF programs, called shields, that harden software without a patch or downtime. The companies say the approach has already mitigated recent Java flaws on an Elasticsearch deployment without interrupting service. Shields are meant to go live only once verified, and humans are expected to review each one before deployment. Cisco's Isovalent, which created Cilium and Tetragon, supplies the foundation for the tool, giving Cisco a commercial interest in wider eBPF adoption. Cisco's Jeetu Patel and OpenAI president Greg Brockman framed the project as a response to attackers who need only one unpatched machine.

stories.headline: Paolo Bulgari, third-generation head of Bulgari jewellery dynasty, dies at 89
stories.claim: Paolo Bulgari, long-serving chairman of the Italian jewellery house Bulgari, has died in Rome aged 89.
stories.summary: Paolo Bulgari, a member of the family behind the Italian jewellery house Bulgari and a key figure in its growth into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged 89. His family announced the death on Saturday 21 November 2026, calling him the greatest jeweller of his time. He joined the family business in 1960 and became chairman in 1984, a post he held alongside his brother Nicola. Under the family, the house expanded into watches, which came to account for around 40 per cent of revenues, as well as perfumes and accessories, and he helped popularise coloured gemstones. Bulgari listed in Milan in 1995 and the family sold its controlling stake to LVMH in 2011 for about €3.7 billion, a move the family called painful but necessary. The family was acquitted of tax evasion charges in 2015, and in 2019 he founded the Paolo Bulgari Foundation with his wife to support education in disadvantaged parts of Rome.

stories.summary: Malaysia plans to send more than 6,500 Myanmar migrants back home in December, the largest announced round so far. stories.headline: Russia buys inflatable planes from China to dupe Ukraine
stories.claim: Russia is reportedly buying cheap inflatable decoy aircraft and tanks from Chinese makers to fool Ukrainian strikes.
stories.summary: Russia is buying inflatable military decoys from Chinese manufacturers, including fake jets, tanks and air defence systems that can cost as little as a few hundred dollars each. The Telegraph traced a supplier, Gauss, which markets its products as radar and heat-signature spoofing kits, and trade data shows Russian imports under a relevant customs code worth at least 10 billion roubles (about £93m) since 2022. Analysts say the decoys make Ukraine waste costly precision munitions, and an RUSI fellow said the suppliers are likely linked to the Chinese military. The reporting raises fresh questions about Beijing's dual-use support for Moscow. Gauss's own promotional videos, aimed at foreign buyers, show factories spanning 16,000 sq m.

stories.headline: Ebikes, screens and failing manners pose challenge for Dutch cycling culture
stories.claim: Dutch cycling culture faces strain from ebikes, screens and poor manners, prompting campaigns and a proposed helmet law.
stories.summary: The Netherlands, long the model of cycling, is struggling with a surge of ebikes, cargo bikes, fatbikes and scooters sharing its 23,000 miles of bike paths. Cyclist deaths rose by more than 50% between 2015 and 2025, according to the Netherlands Institute for Transport Policy Analysis. The Dutch government recently sent a bill to parliament proposing mandatory helmets for under-18s on ebikes, and Leiden has launched an awareness campaign under the slogan 'traffic is a team sport'. Officials and researchers warn that falling activity levels among young people are a public health concern, while others argue cars still cause most harm. The piece is a feature rather than a breaking development, but it highlights a wider policy debate over micromobility.

stories.headline: Fed's Williams says inflation still too high, signals more rate hikes possible
stories.claim: Fed's John Williams says inflation is still too high and more rate hikes may be needed, with a December move likely.
stories.summary: New York Fed president John Williams said on 23 November that US inflation remains too high and must return to the 2% target in a timely and sustained way. He hinted he favours a rate rise at the 8-9 December policy meeting and said he would not rule out raising rates at consecutive meetings if the economy proved strong. Markets broadly expect a quarter-point increase in December, taking the policy range from 3.75-4% higher, with further increases expected in 2027. Governor Christopher Waller has signalled he could back a larger half-point rise given hot price data. The comments came on the same day as a sharp stock rally sparked by Nvidia's leadership news, so the Fed signal sits alongside a strong equity market.

The episode raises the risk of direct confrontation between Nato and Russia.

stories.headline: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict
stories.claim: Analyses of leaked Rosstat records suggest Russian military deaths in Ukraine are far higher than officially acknowledged, at 490,000 or more.
stories.summary: Leaked Russian statistics agency records, analysed by several outlets, suggest the true toll of the war in Ukraine is far higher than officially acknowledged. One analysis puts Russian military deaths at 490,000 or more, while another estimate reported by The New York Times suggests over 700,000 Russian soldiers have died. The Financial Times reports that roughly one in every 17 deaths in Russia since 2022 may be linked to the war, and that Russian soldiers are twice as likely to die by suicide as civilians. The figures rest on leaked Rosstat data and independent analysis, so they are estimates rather than official counts. The findings matter because they challenge the Kremlin's published figures and shed light on the human cost of a conflict that has lasted since 2022.

stories.headline: Seino Holdings works with rivals for better, cleaner transportation
stories.claim: Japanese logistics firm Seino Holdings is partnering with rivals to share delivery networks and raise truck loading efficiency.
stories.summary: Japan's trucking sector has long run parallel delivery networks, with lorries from different companies often covering the same areas. Because shipments are small and return journeys are frequently empty, the loading efficiency of freight vehicles has stayed at roughly 40% of capacity for about 15 years. That waste pushes up costs and makes it harder to cut carbon emissions. Seino Holdings, a major Japanese logistics group, is working with rival firms to pool deliveries and fill more space on each trip. The feature is a reminder that cooperation between competitors may be one of the few practical ways to clean up freight transport in a sector under pressure from driver shortages and emissions targets.

stories.headline: Britain bought fake C4 explosives for Ukraine
stories.claim: An FT investigation finds the UK bought hundreds of tons of an explosive sold as improved C4 for Ukraine, but tests found no RDX.
stories.summary: Britain has spent years buying hundreds of tons of a US-made explosive for Ukraine that was marketed as an improved version of C4, but tests found it contains no RDX, the key ingredient of standard C4, according to a Financial Times investigation. The product, EDC-4, was supplied by Tripwire South LLC, a firm founded by former Pennsylvania police sergeant Ryan Morris. UK Ministry of Defence tests after the first shipment found only PETN, which is more volatile, and an expert warned it is more prone to detonation from heat or friction. Tripwire said there was no safety risk and denied providing false information, while the MoD said the product was fit for purpose. The company's earlier explosives business had gone bankrupt in 2022, and Morris filed for personal bankruptcy in 2024 while already working with the British government.
key_points: UK agreements allowed purchases of up to hundreds of tons of EDC-4 over nearly three years, according to sources.
Tests by the UK Ministry of Defence found no RDX in the explosive, only PETN.

stories.headline: DeepMind’s AI agents found cheaper quantum algorithms, and proved them
stories.claim: Google DeepMind agent teams found much cheaper quantum algorithms for fusion, chemistry and drug design, with results proved in Lean.
stories.summary: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI say teams of Gemini 4 agents have found quantum algorithms that are far cheaper to run for fusion, chemistry and drug-design problems, and proved each result correct in the Lean theorem prover. The biggest gain is a laser-driven fusion fuel calculation that becomes 11.8 times cheaper, with error-corrected qubit needs falling from 5,650 to 4,338. A simulation of a light-sensitive molecule is about eight times cheaper, the cost of simulating Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most medicines, falls 2.5 times, and a widely used maths routine becomes more than 290 times cheaper. The circuits are too large to test on today's machines, which is why formal proofs were used, and an outside checker re-ran every proof to rule out gaming. DeepMind cautions the workloads will still need far more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers will offer, and has open-sourced its Lean library and results.

Wholesale trade, manufacturing and finance drove the expansion, helped by data centre and electronics demand. Retail and food services contracted as residents spent more abroad. The ministry expects slower growth of 2.5-4.5% in 2027 as new AI investment eases from its high level this year, and it warned that elevated energy prices are still feeding global inflation and tighter monetary policy.

stories.summary: A report from DesignVerse, a Bucharest-based enterprise AI startup, finds that general AI coding agents used an organisation's own approved code in fewer than six tasks in ten. Stealthy, non-lethal play earns focus boosts, while headshots and reckless violence push the rating down. Amazon's last successful Leo deployment was 12 weeks ago, on 2 July, aboard a ULA Atlas V rocket. Its main alternatives are grounded: ULA's Vulcan has been out since February after a booster anomaly, and Blue Origin's New Glenn has been down since its only launchpad was destroyed in May. Amazon has also ordered more Ariane 6 launches, but a component issue is expected to disrupt them for the rest of 2026. The FCC has extended Amazon's deadline to launch half of its planned 3,232 satellites, on condition that it moves quickly. SpaceX is meanwhile preparing to launch its first Starlink V3 satellites on Starship.

stories.headline: OpenAI chief scientist proposes industry-wide limits on powerful AI until safety monitoring improves
stories.claim: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed voluntary industry-wide limits on powerful AI until monitoring and safety milestones are met.
stories.summary: OpenAI's chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, has called on AI developers to agree common limits on building increasingly powerful models until researchers can better understand and monitor them. In a blog post published on Sunday, 22 November, he suggested shared thresholds based partly on perplexity, a measure of how well a model predicts text, with developers committing not to cross them until monitoring and safety milestones are reached. He did not specify an initial limit or a start date, and warned that AI could drive fundamental training advances as early as 2027, potentially outpacing safety work. CEO Sam Altman endorsed the idea on X, calling it the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while. The proposal is voluntary rather than regulation, and it lands as US Democrats, who won sweeping midterm victories, prepare to push for tougher AI oversight, setting up a likely clash with President Trump, who has opposed broad AI restrictions.

stories.claim: Former PMs Theresa May and Tony Blair have warned Prime Minister Andy Burnham against rejoining the EU after his Brussels 'reset deal'.
stories.summary: Former prime ministers are warning Andy Burnham against seeking to rejoin the European Union. Theresa May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that she was 'aghast' he is considering it, saying 'Brexit is done' and that he wanted to 'pat people on the head'. Tony Blair said Britain should rejoin only if the EU reforms and embraces technology and innovation, calling Brexit 'a real mistake', while David Cameron said a rejoin conversation would be long and painful. Four of Britain's nine living ex-PMs have now spoken out. The comments follow Burnham's 'reset deal' struck at a Brussels summit on Friday, which gives 100,000 Europeans aged 18 to 31 the right to live, work and study in Britain for up to three years, aligns Britain with EU food and drink safety rules and links emissions trading. Burnham has floated the customs union, single market or a fresh referendum for informal long-term talks, but has ruled out major changes before the next general election, citing Labour's 2024 manifesto. Reform UK called the deal a betrayal, while Kemi Badenoch plans to attack it at a CBI speech and in parliament on Monday.

stories.summary: UN talks in Geneva on lethal autonomous weapons collapsed at about 5am on Saturday without a mandate for a legally binding treaty. All 128 states under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons agreed instead to develop an international instrument over two years, reporting to a 2028 meeting. Russia objected to the agenda on the first day and blocked formal negotiations, and under the consensus rule its objections shaped a much weaker outcome. The US, UK, France, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Turkey and Israel were named by EU diplomats as resisting binding rules, with the US proposing a five-year window for non-binding guidelines. More than 100 states had wanted a new law, and a bloc led by Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama pushed for a treaty within a year. The International Committee of the Red Cross and UN chief António Guterres want a binding instrument, and campaigners called the result a missed opportunity, warning that it may soon be too late to regulate such weapons.

stories.headline: Poundland faces possible administration as owner Gordon Brothers restricts cash
stories.claim: Poundland could collapse into administration despite improved trading, as owner Gordon Brothers restricts cash and weighs a break-up.

Gordon Brothers froze about £50m of cash before releasing around £21m over two weeks, and it is weighing a break-up, which it says would better protect staff. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds have pressed Gordon Brothers for answers.

stories.headline: Delta Atlanta flights delayed by weight-and-balance system failure

Staff used manual workarounds to dispatch aircraft while technicians restored the system, and the disruption reached flights across the US. The FAA said the Delta problem was unrelated to its own air traffic control systems. The incident comes a week after an FAA telecoms failure on 13 November caused a nationwide ground stop of over four hours and about 12,462 cancellations; the agency linked that outage to a router installation at a facility run by L3Harris and paused further installations. United Airlines also delayed departures after a separate outage of its own. The incidents do not share a single confirmed cause, but they have raised questions about the reliability of US aviation infrastructure, and knock-on delays to other carriers are possible if the problem persists.

The city is the centre of the boom, attracting around 60 per cent of US AI venture capital from 2023 to 2025, according to one study, and OpenAI and Anthropic are both based there. stories.headline: Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out
stories.claim: NHS launches a 700,000-woman trial testing whether AI can help read breast cancer screening mammograms.
stories.summary: Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are being invited into what is described as the world's largest trial of artificial intelligence in breast cancer screening. The EDITH trial has started at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 NHS sites, and will run for around three years. Today two NHS specialists read each mammogram; in the trial one of those human readers will be replaced by AI, with AI either grading images before or reviewing them after experts see them. The £11m study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research and led by Warwick and Cambridge with NHS England, with four AI companies involved. Researchers say smaller studies show AI can raise detection rates, but they must confirm it does not cause unnecessary recalls or over-diagnosis of mild disease. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper backed the trial, saying safeguards are needed.

stories.headline: Perplexity's new Monitor API turns web search from a one-off query into a nonstop watchdog

The service has two modes: web monitors that run search queries on a schedule, and page monitors that track up to 10 pages such as pricing or policy pages. Updates are sent by webhook only when a decision model judges them relevant, fresh, credible and new, with a confidence score attached. Perplexity says early internal tests across 60 topics delivered 63 relevant pages in eight hours, against 20 for Firecrawl and 15 for Exa. Pricing is $1 per 1,000 successful web runs or 1,000 fetched URLs, and the service is available now. The launch matters because Perplexity is trying to build revenue beyond consumer search, at a time when Nvidia is reportedly in talks to invest at a valuation above $30 billion.

stories.headline: AI coding agents ace isolated tests but complete fewer than one in ten tasks in a simulated workplace
stories.claim: A new benchmark finds leading AI coding agents fully complete fewer than one in ten tasks in a simulated software workplace.
stories.summary: Leading AI coding agents, including Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, perform well on standard tests but fully complete fewer than one in ten tasks in a new simulated software company. The experiment places the agents as digital employees with colleagues, project boards and chat histories, a setup designed to be closer to real work than isolated benchmarks. The result contrasts with claims that Claude writes more than 80 percent of Anthropic's production code and with SWE-bench being close to saturated. The finding suggests that benchmark scores overstate how ready these tools are to handle full workplace tasks. It is a useful reality check for companies planning to rely on AI agents.

stories.headline: Datacentre bosses met Australian state premiers and ministers almost 120 times in three years, analysis finds
stories.claim: Transparency International finds data-centre firms held almost 120 meetings with Australian state ministers and premiers in three years.
stories.summary: Data-centre companies held almost 120 meetings with premiers and ministers across five Australian states over three years, according to an analysis by Transparency International Australia. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli was the most frequently accessed state leader, with 13 meetings, including three in August and September with NextDC. Political donations from major data-centre firms and their lobbyists nearly tripled, from A$685,000 to A$1.8m, over the same period. The group says the access creates an uneven playing field and calls the figures "just the tip of the iceberg". Amazon Web Services, Macquarie Technology Group and NextDC secured the most ministerial meetings. The findings add pressure on the sector as data-centre expansion faces community opposition.

AWS, Macquarie Technology Group and NextDC had the most ministerial meetings.

stories.headline: The AI Build-Out Is Sucking Up Resources and Crowding Out the Rest of the Economy
stories.claim: Heavy AI spending is drawing workers, equipment, energy and capital away from other industries, raising crowding-out risks.
stories.summary: Big tech spending on AI is now so large that it may be starving the rest of the economy of workers, power, equipment and capital. Some analysts estimate Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia and Meta could spend as much as $1.4 trillion by 2027, while Gartner projects global AI spending will reach $2.5 trillion this year. Goldman Sachs economists warn AI could starve other productive sectors of capital, and Apollo's Torsten Slok expects hyperscaler capex to hit about 3% of GDP a year over 2027 to 2029, against 1.4% in 2025. AI took 65.4% of US venture-capital deal value in 2025, leaving sectors such as biotech under pressure. The piece argues that higher borrowing costs from competition for capital could also choke off other projects, making this a key macro risk.

Morgan Stanley estimates AI capex could add up to 2.5% to US GDP growth this year and over 3% in 2027.

Competition for capital could push borrowing costs up enough to block financing for other sectors.

stories.headline: Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial
stories.claim: Sharjah Architecture Triennial installations map drones and missiles as new constellations in the night sky.
stories.summary: Three domed wood-and-steel installations, thatched and shaped like segments of a giant globe, have gone on show at the Sharjah Architecture Triennial in the UAE. Designed by architect Mohamad Nahleh and professor Ozayr Saloojee, the works are called After Night There is Nothing and map drones, satellites, rockets and missiles as creature-like constellations on their inner curves. The domes sit at three venues: Al Qasimiyah School, a former slaughterhouse and the desert town of Al Madam. The designers present the project as a response to communities living under prolonged military violence, blending modern warfare with myth-making. Traditional Hakawati storytellers will perform at the sites, and the triennial runs from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027.

stories.headline: Jony Ive and Margaret Calvert create posters to celebrate decade of Design Museum in Kensington
stories.claim: Ten designers, including Jony Ive and Tim Burton, made posters marking the Design Museum's 10th anniversary in Kensington.
stories.summary: Ten leading designers have created posters to mark a decade since London's Design Museum opened in its Kensington home on 24 November 2016. The line-up includes Jony Ive with his studio LoveFrom, Tim Burton, Margaret Calvert, Hella Jongerius and Paul Smith, alongside Tom Dixon, Sebastian Conran and others. Calvert's poster riffs on a road-sign fork between Kensington and Shad Thames, the site of the museum's original home from 1989 to 2016. The Kensington building, a Grade II*-listed former Commonwealth Institute, was restored by OMA and Allies and Morrison, with interiors by John Pawson. The posters mark a milestone for a museum that has become a fixture of London's design scene.
